Where it began

Sanjay Vijay Manjrekar was born in Mangalore on 12 July 1965, into a family where Test cricket was the family business. His father, Vijay Manjrekar, played 55 Tests for India between 1952 and 1965.

The young Sanjay came up through the Cooch Behar Trophy as a schoolboy and then played university cricket while studying at Mumbai University. In 1985 his university sides lifted two trophies, the Vizzy and the Rohinton Baria. His first-class debut, for Bombay in a Ranji Trophy quarter-final that March, brought 57 in his only innings and a win.

The player

He was a right-handed middle-order batsman, and he made his Test debut against the West Indies in Delhi late in 1987. His first Test hundred, 108, came against the same opponents in 1989. Later that year, against Pakistan, he made 113 not out in the last innings of a Test to save the match, then 218 later in the same series, the highest score of his career.

In 37 Tests from 1987 to 1996 he scored 2,043 runs at 37.15, with four hundreds and nine fifties, and held 25 catches. He was also part of the India squads that won the Asia Cup in 1990–91 and again in 1995.

What made him special

Run-making came naturally to him at home. In 1990–91 he hit 377 against Hyderabad in a Ranji Trophy semi-final, and he finished his first-class career averaging 55.11. He helped Bombay to the Ranji Trophy in 1994–95 with 224 in the final, and two seasons later led the renamed Mumbai to another title as captain.

He was a careful accumulator rather than a hitter, though he could surprise people: in a one-day international against South Africa he made 105 from 82 balls. His bowling never troubled the Test scorers, and he finished without a wicket, but he did once take a stumping, which is more than most specialist batsmen can say.

Away from the middle

He retired from all cricket in February 1998, choosing a Mumbai match against the touring Australians as his farewell. After that he moved into the commentary box, and talking about the game became his second career, with a batsman's eye for what was happening out in the middle.

And finally

The two Manjrekars, Vijay and Sanjay, played more than ninety Tests for India between them. Few households can have argued about cricket with quite so much authority at the dinner table.
